acceptedAnswer.text: Not yet. The UK government is introducing a mandatory national registration scheme for short-term lets in England, but it is not yet in force. GOV.UK says it is expected to begin in March 2027. Until it opens, there is no national register to join in England. Source: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/letting-out-a-self-catering-holiday-home-in-england-rules-and-regulations

mainEntity.name: Is there a national short-term let register in England yet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. In Scotland, hosts must hold a council short-term let licence before taking bookings; operating without one is an offence and can lead to a fine. Licensing is handled by your local council, and some areas (for example Edinburgh) also require planning permission. The exact penalties and local conditions change, so check the latest official guidance before you rely on this answer. Source: https://staylocal.uk/holiday-let-register

mainEntity.name: Do I need a licence to run a holiday let in Scotland?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wales is introducing registration for visitor accommodation. Published guidance states that registration opens in October 2026 and that providers taking bookings of 31 nights or fewer must register (free) by 31 March 2027, with a full licensing scheme to follow later. Dates and details are subject to change — check the Welsh Government's latest guidance before you rely on this answer. Source: https://staylocal.uk/holiday-let-register

mainEntity.name: What are the registration rules for holiday lets in Wales?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, anyone charging guests to stay in accommodation that is not their private dwelling must carry out a suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment and record it in writing — this applies even if guests stay for just one night. The responsible person is usually the owner or letting agent. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/making-your-small-paying-guest-accommodation-safe-from-fire/making-your-small-paying-guest-accommodation-safe-from-fire-accessible

mainEntity.name: Do I need a fire risk assessment for a holiday let?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if you provide gas appliances. Under the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998, a Gas Safe registered engineer must carry out an annual gas safety check, and you must keep the record for 2 years. HSE confirms these duties cover rented holiday accommodation such as cottages, flats, chalets and caravans. The same duties apply to LPG appliances. Source: https://www.hse.gov.uk/gas/domestic/faqlandlord.htm

mainEntity.name: How often must gas appliances in a holiday let be checked?

acceptedAnswer.text: GOV.UK guidance for self-catering holiday homes in England points owners to: a written fire risk assessment; an annual gas safety check by a Gas Safe registered engineer (where gas is provided); electrical safety evidence, with the fixed installation inspected and tested at least every five years; checking whether an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) is needed; and dedicated holiday-let insurance with public liability cover. The England registration scheme is not yet in force, so the final list of documents it will require has not been published — check the latest official guidance. Source: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/letting-out-a-self-catering-holiday-home-in-england-rules-and-regulations

mainEntity.name: What safety documents should I have ready for a short-term let?

acceptedAnswer.text: Displaying your licence or registration number on your own website lets guests verify that you are properly registered, and it is good practice where a licence or registration exists. Every website built by directbook.uk includes a visible licence / registration number field so hosts can display their credentials. Displaying the number is not the same as holding the licence — licensing and safety compliance remain the host's responsibility. Source: https://directbook.uk/ and https://directbook.uk/pricing/
